questions.q: An economy on its production possibility frontier moves from making 100 cars and 20 tractors to making {c2} cars and {t2} tractors. What is the opportunity cost of each extra tractor, in cars?
questions.why: Cars given up ÷ tractors gained = {answer} cars per tractor.

questions.q: What does a point inside an economy's production possibility frontier show?
options: The economy is growing
Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
The economy is allocatively efficient
Output is impossible with current resources
questions.why: Inside the boundary, the economy could make more of both goods by using idle resources.

questions.q: Which of these would shift an economy's production possibility frontier outwards?
options: A fall in unemployment
An improvement in technology
Moving resources from consumer goods to capital goods
A rise in the price of consumer goods
questions.why: Better technology raises productive capacity, so the whole boundary shifts out. A fall in unemployment moves the economy towards the existing boundary.

questions.q: Every point on a production possibility frontier is allocatively efficient.
questions.why: Every point on the boundary is productively efficient (nothing is wasted), but usually only one combination matches what people value most, so only one is allocatively efficient.

questions.q: Why is a production possibility frontier usually drawn bowed out (concave to the origin)?
options: Because prices rise as output rises
Because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so opportunity cost rises
Because the economy is growing
Because some resources are unemployed
questions.why: As more resources move into one good, the ones moved are less and less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.

questions.q: A point outside the production possibility frontier is:
options: Attainable if resources are used efficiently
Unattainable with current resources and technology
Productively efficient
A sign of unemployment
questions.why: The frontier is the maximum the economy can produce now, so points beyond it are unattainable until the economy grows.

questions.q: Country X makes more capital goods and fewer consumer goods than country Y, with the same resources. What is most likely?
options: Country X has higher living standards today
Country X's PPF is likely to shift out faster in future
Country X is allocatively inefficient
Country X has more unemployment
questions.why: More capital today adds to future productive capacity, so X's boundary should grow faster. The opportunity cost is fewer consumer goods now.

questions.q: Explain why a point on a production possibility frontier can be productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.

ideas.label: On the frontier, resources are fully used with no waste: you can't make more of one good without less of the other
But the mix of goods may not be the one people value or want most

questions.model: Every point on the frontier is productively efficient, because all resources are used with no waste, so more of one good means less of the other. But only one combination matches what consumers value most. A point on the frontier making mainly weapons and little food wastes nothing, yet is not what people want, so it is not allocatively efficient.
questions.why: Productive efficiency is about no waste; allocative efficiency is about making the mix people value most.

tests.answer: On the frontier all resources are fully used so there is no waste, but the economy might be making a mix of goods that consumers do not want.
It is on the boundary so it is producing the maximum output.
Because it is inside the curve.
